# Scope and Objections {#sec-scope-objections}

**Locus, not degree (O1).** This paper formalizes *where* verification
fails and *why*, in three exhaustive cases. It does not formalize how
much trust a failure costs in any graded sense — a single admitted
signer and a globally corrupt certificate authority are the same
determination-failure cell, distinguished only by how badly the
admitted trust can be abused, which is a question this model does not
ask.

**Reliance-structure, not trust-proper (O3).** What is formalized is the
structural precondition for trust — an unverifiable gap that something
must fill — not trust as a psychological or social attitude in the sense
the philosophy-of-trust literature studies it (@sec-related-work). This
paper is conceded ground, not a hidden weakness: it formalizes the
*reliance* a rational agent is forced into once verification is
exhausted, which is necessary for, but does not by itself constitute,
trust in the fuller sense that literature uses the word.

**Necessary versus elective trust (O4).** The trichotomy characterizes
trust that is *forced* — there is no scheme, at any stratum, for the
claim in question. It says nothing about *elective* trust, where a
verifier could in principle check a claim but chooses reliance instead
for cost or convenience reasons. Both are real; only the forced kind is
this paper's object.

## Model adequacy (W1)

The sharpest exposure of a result this abstract is whether its
definitions are actually the right ones — convergent validity, argued
on three independent prongs, rather than asserted from the definitions
alone.

First, each definition has an independently-adequate home outside this
paper: monotonicity's upward-closed outcomes are exactly Complete CALM's
monotone specifications [@hellerstein-2026]; certifiability's
semi-decidable class is exactly the affirmable-properties tradition of
synthetic topology [@escardo-2004]; determination, given a mechanism, is
exactly the finding archival diplomatics reports from case-study
evidence [@interpares-2002].

Second, the instances bite on real systems: the light surety-ceiling
witness, the identity domain, and — most concretely — the split-view
reduction of @sec-instances, which predicts a transparency log's actual
deployed defenses rather than merely classifying the attack after the
fact.

Third, and most directly: the framework *derives* a result rather than
merely accommodating one. The claim in @sec-instances that a failed axis
names a specific trust anchor — signer, voucher, witness quorum — is
itself an adequacy check, because it recovers, from first principles,
exactly the anchor inventory that deployed practice converged on by
other means.

## What was searched, and what was not (honest scope statement)

The related-work sweep behind @sec-related-work reached arXiv, open
bibliographic indices, author-hosted PDFs, institutional repositories,
and the Internet Archive. Several major venues remained hostile across
repeated attempts — paywalled philosophy-of-trust archives, several
publisher search interfaces, and citation-graph APIs that rate-limited
every attempt. Two consequences follow, stated plainly rather than left
for a reviewer to discover: post-2022 philosophy-of-trust literature is
effectively unsampled, and several of the negative findings below rest
on an exhaustive check of *one document each*, which closes that
document, not the literature it sits in.

Absence of a hit under these conditions is not claimed as proof of
absence — it is the expected observation for a genuine unification
claim. If this composition had already been published, it would likely
be known in the subfields it draws from, several of which are
well-studied and actively cited. What @sec-related-work offers instead
of a clean-room "we searched and found nothing" is the closest prior art
found at each of five clusters, with the specific line that distinguishes
this paper's claim from each — the shape a well-read related-work
section takes, not the shape a defensive one takes.

## Future work

**A diagnostic lens for alignment, not a formalization (C3).** The three
axes give a diagnostic vocabulary for why a machine-learned model's
alignment resists verification, and it is worth naming precisely because
it hits all three at once rather than one: a model's behavior is not
*determined* by anything a verifier can commit to in advance (behavior
on unseen inputs is not a function of any finite training record); it is
not *certifiable* even in principle, by Rice's theorem applied to
semantic behavioral properties; and any alignment claim stated as a
universal over an open input space is not *monotone* — one adversarial
input can falsify it after arbitrarily much confirming evidence. This is
offered as a one-paragraph diagnostic mention, deliberately not pursued
further here: turning it into a formal result first requires pinning
down what "aligned" means as a claim in this paper's sense, which is
future work in its own right and would sidetrack the introduction if
attempted now.

**The full surety ceiling (the axios follow-up).** @sec-instances
includes a deliberately light, zero-frontier-machinery witness of the
verification ceiling's build-domain specialization, the **surety
ceiling**. The full treatment — corroboration quorums, format/parse
gates, and the forced-generator tightness results resting on Rice and
Rice–Shapiro that the light witness omits by design — is empirical,
conditional in places, and prose-grade rather than machine-checked
throughout; it is the subject of a separate, follow-up paper on
source-build integrity (the axios project), cited from this paper but
not included in it, so that this paper's own epistemic grade stays
uniformly machine-checked.
